extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, computer scientists, and general readers interested in AI and automated theorem proving
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for what counts as a mathematical proof and for judging/comparing computerized theorem provers (ATPs, ITPs, and hybrid ML-guided systems), including correctness, understandability, formalizability, novelty of conjectures, and pedagogical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is a step-by-step logical argument that verifies the truth of a conjecture and explains why it’s true; once it’s proved, a conjecture becomes a theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes both verification (establishing validity) and explanation (showing why). Use of this definition distinguishes mere computational checks from genuinely explanatory arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human understandability / explainability
rubrics_metrics.description: A good proof should explain its reasoning in a way that people can understand; machine proofs that are inscrutable to humans (e.g., ATP output that looks like uninterpretable data) fail this criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: ATP-produced proofs can look like long strings of data that no human can follow; ITPs tend to produce proof-level techniques a human can sit down and understand. Desirable provers produce human-seeming structure and explanations, not only correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal correctness and verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be formally checkable and verified by theorem provers (ATPs/ITPs) to ensure correctness and catch errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: formal verification revealed errors in Hales’s original Kepler proof; computer-checked proofs such as the four-color theorem, Kepler conjecture, and Boolean Pythagorean triples problem provide high confidence even when long or complex. Formal verifiability is a separate axis from human explainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness / filling in gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: A rigorous proof must fill in logical gaps and provide step-by-step deduction rather than relying on omitted intermediate steps or intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof assistants force authors to be explicit about needed lemmas and assumptions; they are valuable for catching hidden mistakes or unstated steps (Voevodsky and others used computers to find such errors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalizability / expressibility in computer-friendly language
rubrics_metrics.description: For machines to check or generate proofs, the mathematical problem must be expressed in a formal language that the prover accepts; the ease or difficulty of that formalization is a practical criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: problems that require excessive reframing or coding such that 'by the time I’ve reframed my question... I would have solved the problem myself.' The cost of formalization can limit adoption among mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness / interest of generated conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatically generated conjectures should be novel and interesting (not trivial or mere duplicates) and ideally lead to provable, nontrivial theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Urban’s neural-net-generated formulas produced tens of thousands of candidates, many duplicates, and relatively few provable/interesting conjectures. Evaluation should check novelty, provability, and mathematical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of deductive rigor and inductive insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Good theorem-proving systems (and proofs) should capture both deductive, step-by-step logic and the inductive, intuition-driven generation of conjectures and strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that conjectures typically arise from inductive intuition while proofs rely on deductive methods; successful automation aims to marry both (e.g., ML-guided provers that learn from experience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication — bridging human and machine language
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable prover should bridge the communication barrier between human mathematical language and machine formalism, enabling proofs that both verify and communicate ideas in familiar structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Szegedy and others point to natural language processing and language models as routes to make machine proofs more human-seeming; evaluation should consider how well systems present proofs in forms humans can grasp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical value / forcing clear organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Using theorem provers can be judged by their utility as teaching tools: they force students to be organized and to think clearly about the logical structure of proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emily Riehl’s courses demonstrate that proof assistants help novices understand what they need and the logical dependencies. Evaluate by whether the tool helps learners produce correct, well-structured proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability and manageability of proof artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof’s practicality includes whether its formal representation is of manageable size and can be inspected or stored; proofs that are terabytes large or otherwise uninspectable are problematic for human consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: some machine-generated proofs (e.g., early Boolean Pythagorean triples proof variants) produced enormous artifacts (hundreds of gigabytes/terabytes) that are impractical to examine; prefer proofs that balance thoroughness with tractable representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of learning with reasoning (ML-guided proving)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern evaluation should consider whether systems effectively integrate machine learning to guide search and improve the efficiency and creativity of theorem proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Urban’s and Google Research’s efforts combine ATP/ITP technology with neural networks and language models; assessment should measure gains in efficiency, ability to generate provable conjectures, and the quality of resulting proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural similarity to human proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A promising criterion is whether machine proofs exhibit networked or tree-like structures similar to those produced by people, which may make them easier to interpret and reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DeDeo and Viteri found that machine and human proofs share networked structures; systems that produce proofs with recognizable higher-level techniques are more likely to be adopted by mathematicians.
